title: A queen lost on move 13 comes back to mate
summary: A-White lost its queen to Bxd5 early on board A, and B-White dropped it on a4, where it stood for most of the game. B-Black was ahead on board B by the engine's count through the second half, and board A swung to White after the queens were traded on e1 at moves 30 and 31. At the end B-Black's N@c3+ and Nxa4+ won that queen back, and A-White, who sat a moment to wait for it, mated with Q@b8#.
event: HypeBeast 1.1.1 against itself, 500,000 nodes a move for one team and 450,000 for the other

result.text: White on board A mates; the team of A-White and B-Black wins.

moves.note: Bxd5 wins A-White's queen for a knight, and the queen goes to B-White on board B. Follow it: B-White drops it on a4 at move 18, it stands there until Nxa4+ at move 37, and that capture hands it back to A-White for the mate.

Black had just taken the knight on f6 with the queen. Its first choice was B@d7+, checking first and taking the queen a move later. It took at once instead, which puts the queen in B-Black's hand straight away, and it rated the immediate capture better if a pawn or a knight reached it from board B. A knight did, from Nxe5 there, and B-Black dropped the queen as Q@e7 at move 15.

lines.note: The engine's expected reply: Black drops bishops and trades on d2, about four pawns in Black's favour by its count.
Its first choice: check with B@d7+ and take the queen one move later.

moves.note: Its first choice was Bxc4. Castling long leaves the bishop on d5 to cxd5, but by the engine's count a bishop in B-Black's hand was worth only about a pawn there, and it expected a pawn from board B, about three chances in four. With that pawn in hand it rated O-O-O well above Bxc4. The pawn came at once, from exf7+, and two moves later Black's count was nearly nine pawns ahead, though the board swung back later.

lines.note: White takes the bishop, which goes to B-Black, and Rxd5 wins back a pawn; a search of White's answer scored the position about two and a half pawns for White.
Its first choice, taking the pawn on c4 with the bishop.

moves.note: B-White drops the queen won by Bxd5 on board A. Three moves earlier its first choice had been to drop it on e2 with check; it played Qe2+ with the queen already on the board and kept this one in hand. The queen stays on a4 for the rest of the game, and its capture is what ends it.
A pawn dropped on d7 with check. It stays there until move 37, when d8=R+ promotes it, and that rook's capture Rxb8+ starts the final attack.

Its first choice was P@c3+, but in that line the knight on c7 survives and later takes the rook on a8 with Nxa8+, and by the engine's count a rook in A-Black's hand was enough to mate on board A. Qxc7 removes the knight at once. It rated Qxc7 far better if a pawn reached White, about an even chance, and one did, from Bxc3 on board A. The knight went to A-White, who dropped one on c5 two moves later.

lines.note: After Qxc7 the engine's line still has Black about six and a half pawns ahead by its count.
Its first choice: the knight on c7 is left alone and ends the line with Nxa8+, taking the rook.

moves.note: Its first choice was Qxd1, taking Black's queen. It dropped a knight on c5 instead (one had just come from Qxc7 on board B), rating it nearly as good if nothing arrived and much better if a bishop came from board B. No bishop came, and Black traded queens with Qxe1+ Bxe1, which put a queen in each hand on board B. The knight stayed on c5 until Nd7+ at move 39, two moves before the mate.

lines.note: Black's expected answer trades queens on e1, sending a queen to each side on board B.
Its first choice: take the queen on d1, after which the e2 pawn recaptures and promotes with check.

moves.note: N@e2+ checks, and its own line expected Kb1 and Ngxe3, exactly what followed. Meanwhile the queens were traded on e1 on board A, so both sides here got a queen. The engine had given that about one chance in nine, and in that case it rated N@e2+ the worst of the five moves it compared; its score at the next turn was far lower. Searched the same way, though, N@e2+ still scored above both alternatives listed, so whether it was a mistake stays open.

lines.note: Its own line: Kb1 and Ngxe3, as played.
A search that ignores the other board takes on e3 at once; searched the same way, that scored far below N@e2+.
A longer search preferred P@c3, but scored it lower than N@e2+ when both were searched the same way.
White's own line at its next turn, with the queen from board A in hand: about one pawn in White's favour by its count.

moves.note: Bxe1 completes the queen trade on e1. Qxe1+ took the queen A-White had dropped there (it came from Nxb5 on board B), and Bxe1 takes Black's queen, so a queen goes to each side on board B. From here board A is in White's favour by both sides' count to the end.

Ngxe3 takes the bishop on e3, and the bishop goes to A-White, who dropped it as B@f2 at move 32. By the engine's count it was the best or close to the best move whatever arrived. Its score fell sharply at its next turn, after P@a7+ and Kxa7, but White's own count a move later still had Black slightly ahead, and nothing in its lines explains the drop.

lines.note: Its own line expected Q@e8+ with the queen White had just received from board A.
White's own line at its next turn, after the pawn from Bxe3+ arrived, scored about three pawns for White.

moves.note: The pawn came from Bxe3+ on board A. Its first choice was Q@e8+, but it expected a knight from board A, about three chances in five, and with a knight to follow up with N@b5+ it rated P@a7+ far higher. No knight came. A search that ignores the other board dropped the queen on d7 instead and, searched the same way, scored it about four pawns better than P@a7+.

lines.note: The engine's expected answer: Black takes the pawn with Kxa7, which sends it to A-White.
Its first choice, Q@e8+ with the queen from board A.
A search that ignores the other board plays Q@d7, scored about four pawns better than P@a7+ by the same kind of search.
If a knight had come: N@b5+ follows and wins the queen on c7 and the rook on a8, about sixteen pawns for White by its count.

moves.note: Black was lost on this board by its own count, more than twelve pawns down. Its first choice was N@h3+; it switched to N@e2+ because it expected a queen to reach it from board B, about three chances in four, and with a queen in hand it rated N@e2+ much better. The queen came, from Rxd1 on board B, and was dropped as Q@b6 at move 35, where Nd7+ later attacked it.

lines.note: White's expected answer takes the knight with Rxe2, and the engine still scores White about fifteen pawns ahead.
Its first choice, N@h3+, which White takes with gxh3.

moves.note: White on board B was lost by its own count, about 38 pawns down, but only about seven of those were on this board. The rest is what its losses would hand to board A: its line lets Black take the queen on a4 and the rook on e8, and by its count either piece in A-White's hand was enough to mate there. It rated f8=Q nearly the same as f8=R if nothing arrived.

lines.note: Its own line: Bxf8 takes the new rook at once, and later bxa4 and Rxe8 take the queen and a rook, the captures that cost it most by its count.
A search that ignores the other board plays Qxa6+, which it scores a little better, but bxa6 would hand the queen to A-White, enough to mate there by the engine's count.
With a pawn arriving for White and a knight for Black, it would drop the queen on a5, and Black answers N@c3+, the drop that was played.

moves.note: The rook, promoted from the d7 pawn the move before, takes the knight that blocked on b8 and sends it to B-Black, who drops it at once as N@c3+. When Kxb8 takes the rook, it reaches board B only as a pawn. The engine scored this board about 87 pawns ahead even if nothing arrived, and it expected a rook from board B, about four chances in five, with which N@d7+ and R@b8+ mate by its count.

lines.note: Its own line after Kxb8, with White still far ahead by its count.
If a rook had come from board B: Rxb8+ Kxb8 N@d7+ Kc8 R@b8+, a forced mate by its count.

moves.note: B-Black drops the knight just won by Rxb8+ on board A. Its line shows the point: bxc3 Nxc3+ Kb2 Nxa4+ takes the queen on a4, and by the engine's count a queen in A-White's hand was enough to mate. That queen was A-White's own, lost to Bxd5 at move 13 and dropped on a4 by B-White at move 18. It also weighed Rxe8, taking a rook, also enough to mate by its count, and rated N@c3+ slightly higher.

The only legal move. White is lost here by its own count, about fifty pawns, and most of that is what its losses hand to board A, where by its count the queen on a4 or a rook would mate in A-White's hand. Its line shows Nxc3+ and Nxa4+ next, as happened.

The knight dropped on c5 at move 30 checks from d7 and attacks the queen on b6. The engine expected rooks to be traded on board B, about two chances in three, and with a rook in hand Nd7+ mated by its count. A search that ignores the other board played Bxb7, which searched the same way scored far lower. What came instead was the queen from a4, by Nxc3+ and Nxa4+.

lines.note: Its own line expected Ka8 and Nxb6+, taking the queen; Black played Kc8 instead.
A search that ignores the other board plays Bxb7, which scored far lower than Nd7+ searched the same way.
With a rook from board B: N@d7+ Kc8 R@b8+, mate by its count.

moves.note: A-White sat for about a second: on board B its partner, on move, could take the queen on a4, and a queen dropped on b8 mates. Nxa4+ came, and Q@b8# ended the game with the queen A-White had lost on this board at move 13.

lines.note: Had Black been given a move instead of the sit, the engine's line has its checks running out with White still about 27 pawns ahead.
